heading: A structural class of explanatory creativity, with selected and constructed correspondence
text: ## A structural class of explanatory creativity, with selected and constructed correspondence
# Part 0 — Read this first

label: Two words, as used here
text: **Two words, as used here.** An **argument** is, in the owner's words, "reasons why this and not that": "something that can be strung together into a coherent structure to decide why this and not another."

label: Two words, as used here
text: Each of its steps is of an inference form that the person using it admits (\(\operatorname{Form}_j\), Part IX), and admitting a form, like accepting a claim, is tentative; for that person, while the form stays admitted, the step rules out the case in which its premises are met and its conclusion fails.

label: Two words, as used here
text: An argument rules out a claim when the claim is inconsistent with its conclusion and the claim's denial is not among its premises, in the structural sense of Part IX.

label: Two words, as used here
text: An argument is never a reason *for* a claim: what it does is rule out a claim's denial, or a rival, for someone who can use it, and only while it stays usable (K2).

label: Two words, as used here
text: A claim that no argument rules out is only not ruled out, and gets nothing from that; a claim whose denial an argument rules out gets nothing more than that ruling out.

label: Two words, as used here
text: To **tentatively accept** a claim is a person's choice to go on with it, made, in the owner's words, "for whatever reason"; whatever is accepted is accepted tentatively, open to being dropped, and the semantics never defines accepting by the arguments someone holds.

label: Two words, as used here
text: A premise of an argument can be a claim tentatively accepted as given, and an argument need not cite a test (Part IX).

label: Two words, as used here
text: Nothing in the semantics is settled: whether a candidate meets the conditions of an account depends on the candidate, its question and its target, not on anyone's view of them, and whatever anyone accepts about it is accepted tentatively (Part VI); in the owner's words, "A theory is never settled."

label: Two words, as used here
text: Where a claim taken as given is used to rule out a rival, that ruling out is a choice the person made, not something the claim does by itself; in the owner's words, "That "ruling out" is a choice that was made."

heading: What this document claims
text: ## What this document claims

heading: What this document claims
text: An explanation is a **question-relevant organization of dependencies**, held to a target by a **transport** that is tested only by **what changes when things are changed**.

heading: What this document claims
text: The definition never asks whether a piece of the explanation "is the same kind of thing" as a piece of the world.

heading: What this document claims
text: That question has no independent content: at any level of detail, a *kind* is nothing over and above how a component responds to the changes that level admits.

heading: What this document claims
text: Two components no admitted change can separate are one kind at that level, whatever labels anyone attaches to them (Part II, Argument 1).

heading: What this document claims
text: Correspondence between a representation and what it represents is not an import here.

heading: What this document claims
text: It is a **relation with a provenance**.

heading: What this document claims
text: A correspondence can be *selected*, produced by variation and survival on a history of encountered changes, with no represented target in that history; or *constructed*, produced by an episode of conjecture and criticism; or merely *declared* by whoever writes the model down.

heading: What this document claims
text: The three are told apart by their histories, not their outputs, and the semantics keeps them apart (Part IV).

heading: What this document claims
text: Creativity lives in construction.

heading: What this document claims
text: Selection produces the raw material construction works on.

heading: What this document claims
text: Declaration is used only as a modelling convenience, and a claim about creativity cannot depend on it.

heading: What this document claims
text: Questions have provenance too.

heading: What this document claims
text: A question, meaning its target, its scope of admitted changes and what it asks, can be found as well as answered, and the semantics represents both (Part III, Argument 5).

heading: What this document claims
text: This is what separates it from any class in which questions are inputs: such a class cannot represent question-finding, and creativity includes finding questions, not only answering them.

heading: What this document claims
text: The **constitutive conjecture** is this: explanatory creativity is fully characterized by (i) organizations and the changes they admit, (ii) transports between organizations tested by change-fidelity alone, (iii) the provenance of those transports and of the questions they serve, and (iv) their physical realization, the instantiation and transformation of these contents in carriers (Part I).

heading: What this document claims
text: A candidate would conflict with the conjecture if an argument not using these four ruled out the claim that it is a non-explanation of its question while these four cannot represent it; so would a candidate that meets (E) on its question and contract (Part V) when such an argument rules out the claim that it is an explanation there.

heading: What this document claims
text: An argument that exhibits either rules the conjecture out for whoever can use it, while it stays usable.

heading: What this document claims
text: Part XV lists what such an argument would have to exhibit.

heading: What this document does not claim
text: ## What this document does not claim

heading: What this document does not claim
text: It does not define reference in terms of uninterpreted matter.

heading: What this document does not claim
text: It defines reference in terms of matter **plus a selection or construction history**.

heading: What this document does not claim
text: Physics says what organization a lump of matter instantiates; history says how that organization came to track another.

heading: What this document does not claim
text: Neither alone yields representation.

heading: What this document does not claim
text: It does not say prediction is explanation.

heading: What this document does not claim
text: Fidelity is over **component structure under change**, not over outputs.

heading: What this document does not claim
text: Two systems with identical outputs and different internal routes are different organizations here, and the semantics says so (Argument 9).

heading: What this document does not claim
text: It does not supply an aesthetics independent of any declared appraisal, a probability on claims, an appraisal of its own, or a function that orders explanations or thinkers.

heading: What this document does not claim
text: Where a claim needs one of these, the semantics does not supply it and marks the place: a claim that invokes an appraisal or aesthetic value takes the appraisal relation as an input (Parts XI, XIV), and a claim that needs any of the others is left open (Part XIV).

heading: What this document does not claim
text: It does not attribute an achievement to contributors beyond what a history contains (Part XI).

heading: What this document does not claim
text: It does not decide whether any human, machine, institution or lineage belongs to the classes defined.

heading: What this document does not claim
text: It defines the classes.

heading: What is imported, what is an index, and what is defined
text: ## What is imported, what is an index, and what is defined

heading: What is imported, what is an index, and what is defined
text: The semantics has two imports: the **physical module** \(\Theta\), which says what organization a physical occurrence instantiates at a grain, and the **appraisal relation** \(\mathcal N\), taken as an input wherever a question invokes an appraisal.

heading: What is imported, what is an index, and what is defined
text: Grain, boundary, continuity and the contract of admitted changes are **declared indices**: every claim is relative to them, and none is a predicate that a case meets or fails.

heading: What is imported, what is an index, and what is defined
text: Everything else is defined in terms of the two imports, the structural vocabulary of (O) and (Q), the declared indices and the **declared inputs**, in the order Part XIV states.

heading: What is imported, what is an index, and what is defined
text: No undefined predicate that says "explains" without a question and a contract, or "is a cause", is taken as an import, and no definition depends on one (Argument 6); (EX) is a defined relation of an episode, not such a predicate.

# Part I — Commitments

label: Faithfulness without assessors
text: **Faithfulness without assessors.** Whether a transport is faithful on a contract is independent of whether anyone tentatively accepts it.

label: Faithfulness without assessors
text: Systems can be in error about their transports, their observations, their criticisms and their own capacities.

label: Fallibility without error-as-work
text: **Fallibility without error-as-work.** A theory may contain a faithful scoped dependence together with errors elsewhere.

label: Fallibility without error-as-work
text: What cannot count as explanation is an error in the very dependence alleged to do the work.

label: Fallibility without error-as-work
text: "Explanation" in this commitment means an account, an explanatory candidate meeting \(\operatorname{Account}\) on its contract (Part V); a theory in error offered as an answer is an explanatory candidate, which ordinary usage may still call an explanation, and whether an account is easy to vary is a separate matter (Part VI).

label: Conjecture, criticism, action
text: **Conjecture, criticism, action.** An idea may be entertained with no argument that rules out its rivals.

label: Conjecture, criticism, action
text: A criticism has a target and is itself conjectural.

label: Conjecture, criticism, action
text: A thinker may act on an appraisal that no argument has decided.

label: Recursive scrutiny with operative return
text: **Recursive scrutiny with operative return.** Any aspect of a system's practice, a question, a contract, a transport, a method, an attention policy, can become a target, and the result must be able to change how the system proceeds.

label: Substrate independence with physical conditions
text: **Substrate independence with physical conditions.** Any carrier may bear an organization.

label: Substrate independence with physical conditions
text: Every attribution of an organization to a physical system is a claim that the system instantiates it, and whether a system can is a matter of physics; here and throughout, to adopt something is to take it tentatively, open to replacement, and an attribution that the adopted physics excludes conflicts with it, as a candidate can conflict with a claim (Part VI).

label: Substrate independence with physical conditions
text: That an organization admits an edit is not a claim that the edit can be carried out or can come about, so an attribution does not conflict with a physics that excludes carrying out an edit the attributed organization admits (Parts II and III).

label: Substrate independence with physical conditions
text: Which organizations a carrier can bear, and whether what carriers of one physical medium bear can pass to carriers of another, are matters of physics as well, and substrate independence reaches as far as contents can pass between media.

label: Substrate independence with physical conditions
text: Where two media cannot exchange what they bear, the contents that only one of them can bear form, for a system built of the other, a barrier in the sense of Part XIII.

label: Substrate independence with physical conditions
text: Physical possibility enters the semantics where a content is instantiated in a carrier or transformed, as when it is held, copied, taught, tested, built or performed (Parts IV and X to XIII), and it also enters as the content of claims that a candidate can conflict with (Part VI).

label: Substrate independence with physical conditions
text: It does not define a question, its range of changes, an account or a conflict between candidates (Parts III, V, VI).

label: Two provenances, not one
text: **Two provenances, not one.** Selection and construction both produce correspondences.

label: Two provenances, not one
text: They are distinguished by their histories.

label: Two provenances, not one
text: Neither is reduced to the other.

text: **Tasks.** A substrate is a physical system; an attribute a set of its states; a task a specified input-to-output attribute transformation with explicit resources and side effects.

label: (Suff) Sufficiency
text: Part V says which of the four each classic attempt fails: a table of observed answers fails (F1); a reversed calculation fails (F2) under the production contract; conclusion-as-premise fails non-circular dependence.

part: Part XV — What would rule this class out
label: (Suff) Sufficiency
text: A table that encodes the response to every admitted change does not fail (F1); like any new attempt, it is a counterexample only if it fails none of the four and such an argument rules out the claim that it is an explanation.

part: Part XV — What would rule this class out
label: (Nec) Necessity
text: **(Nec) Necessity.** A candidate such that an argument not using (E) rules out the claim that it is a non-explanation, whose organization no transport can preserve under any contract on its target.

part: Part XV — What would rule this class out
label: (Nec) Necessity
text: Eliminative explanation (Part VII) is the exposed case.

part: Part XV — What would rule this class out
label: (Elim) Reinstatement of kinds
text: **(Elim) Reinstatement of kinds.** A case where a kind-label distinguishes two accounts that no admitted change distinguishes, and the distinction does explanatory work.

part: Part XV — What would rule this class out
label: (Elim) Reinstatement of kinds
text: An argument that exhibits such a case would rule out the Consequence of Argument 1, for whoever can use it, and make correspondence an import again.

part: Part XV — What would rule this class out
label: (Prov) Genesis
text: **(Prov) Genesis.** Any of three: a selected transport whose value at an unseen change is determined by its history although its population admits a differing survivor there (against Argument 3; a population with no such survivor is the claim's own qualification, not an argument that rules it out); a method that rewrites every construction trace as a selection history without loss (against Part IV, collapsing the two provenances and removing creativity from the semantics); or an argument that rules out that explanation operates on the object layer of Part IV.

part: Part XV — What would rule this class out
label: (QF) Question-finding
text: **(QF) Question-finding.** A case of finding a new question that treating a contract as a content, something that can be constructed, be new, and be the originative contribution of an episode, fails to capture; or an episode that is not creative which that treatment counts as creative (against Argument 5).

part: Part XV — What would rule this class out
label: A mathematical error
text: **A mathematical error.** A counterexample to the finite monotone claim, (I2), (O1), (T2), (CT2), or Arguments 1–3 under their stated assumptions.
# Part XVI — Arguments

heading: 1. Kind preservation needs no condition of its own
text: ## 1. Kind preservation needs no condition of its own

heading: 1. Kind preservation needs no condition of its own
label: Claim
text: **Claim.** If a transport meets (F1) on \(C\), no active component \(k\) of \(E\) has a signature on \(\tau[C]\) that differs from the one its counterpart \(\lambda(k)\) has on \(C\), up to the port translation.

heading: 1. Kind preservation needs no condition of its own
text: *Why this and not its denial.*

heading: 1. Kind preservation needs no condition of its own
text: By (K), \(\operatorname{sig}_C(\lambda(k))=\{(a,b,\operatorname{proj}^{\lambda}_{V_k}\operatorname{Sol}_{\lambda(k)}(a,b))\}\) and \(\operatorname{sig}_{\tau[C]}(k)=\{(\tau(a),\sigma(b),L_k(\tau(a),\sigma(b)))\}\).

heading: 1. Kind preservation needs no condition of its own
text: (F1) equates the third coordinates pointwise. ∎

heading: 1. Kind preservation needs no condition of its own
label: Consequence
text: **Consequence.** A condition "each component's counterpart must be a component of the same kind" adds nothing to (F1) on any contract.

heading: 1. Kind preservation needs no condition of its own
label: Consequence
text: Where the contract separates two kinds, (F1) already distinguishes them; where it does not, they are one kind on that contract.

heading: 1. Kind preservation needs no condition of its own
label: Consequence
text: The word "kind" is therefore eliminable from the definition of an account, and its elimination loses no case.

heading: 2. Same counterparts, one account
text: ## 2. Same counterparts, one account

heading: 2. Same counterparts, one account
label: Claim
text: **Claim.** Let \(\mathcal E,\mathcal E'\) be candidates for the same \(p\) that both meet (F1), (F2) and (A) on \(C\).

heading: 2. Same counterparts, one account
label: Claim
text: (i) Their answer profiles coincide on \(C\).

heading: 2. Same counterparts, one account
label: Claim
text: (ii) If a bijection \(\varphi\) of their active components gives each \(k\) and \(\varphi(k)\) one counterpart, the same subnetwork of \(D\) with port translations that are bijections onto the same ports of \(D\), then \(k\) and \(\varphi(k)\) are of one kind on \(C\) for every \(k\); so far as (F1), (F2) and (A) reach, the two are one account on \(C\): \(\varphi\) pairs their active components, each pair of one kind on \(C\), and by (i) their answer profiles coincide.

heading: 2. Same counterparts, one account
text: *Why this and not its denial.*

heading: 2. Same counterparts, one account
text: (i) By (A), \(\operatorname{Ans}_E(\tau(a),\sigma(b))=\operatorname{Ans}_p(a,b)=\operatorname{Ans}_{E'}(\tau'(a),\sigma'(b))\) for every \((a,b)\in C\).

heading: 2. Same counterparts, one account
text: (ii) By Argument 1, \(k\) has the signature of its counterpart on the ports its translation names, and \(\varphi(k)\) the signature of the same counterpart on the same ports; composing the one translation with the inverse of the other gives a footprint bijection under which the two signatures, read on \(C\), coincide. ∎

heading: 2. Same counterparts, one account
text: Without the premise of (ii) nothing more follows: candidates whose counterparts are different subnetworks, or cut \(D\) at different places, are different candidates with one answer profile (Argument 9; Part VI, redundant routes).

heading: 2. Same counterparts, one account
text: A coarsening is not a recoding (Argument 8).

heading: 2. Same counterparts, one account
label: Consequence
text: **Consequence.** Where two candidates that meet (F1), (F2) and (A) differ only in which component has which counterpart, the contract does not contain the distinction; a claim that the target pairs its components one way and not the other is a claim that some admitted change separates them, and must supply it.

heading: 2. Same counterparts, one account
label: Consequence
text: A finer contract that contains such a change is a new question (Part III); whether anyone asks it is that person's choice (Part 0).

heading: 3. Selected transports are underdetermined on unseen changes their population leaves open
text: ## 3. Selected transports are underdetermined on unseen changes their population leaves open

heading: 3. Selected transports are underdetermined on unseen changes their population leaves open
label: Claim
text: **Claim.** Let \(t\) be selected from a population \(\mathcal T\) on a finite history \(H\subsetneq C\).

heading: 3. Selected transports are underdetermined on unseen changes their population leaves open
label: Claim
text: For every \((a,b)\in C\setminus H\) at which some \(t'\in\mathcal T\), also surviving on \(H\), has a different value from \(t\), the value of \(t\) at \((a,b)\) is underdetermined by \(H\): survival on \(H\) does not distinguish \(t\) from \(t'\) there.

heading: 3. Selected transports are underdetermined on unseen changes their population leaves open
label: Claim
text: The presence of an unseen pair alone leaves open whether such a \(t'\) exists; it must be a member of \(\mathcal T\), a transport the physics and the stated construction admit (Part XII), and it must survive on \(H\) (Part IV).

heading: 3. Selected transports are underdetermined on unseen changes their population leaves open
text: *Why this and not its denial.*

heading: 3. Selected transports are underdetermined on unseen changes their population leaves open
text: The component relations \(L_j(a,b)\) are supplied independently for each \((a,b)\).

heading: 3. Selected transports are underdetermined on unseen changes their population leaves open
text: Survival on \(H\) constrains only \(\{L_j(a,b):(a,b)\in H\}\).

heading: 3. Selected transports are underdetermined on unseen changes their population leaves open
text: Where \(\mathcal T\) contains a transport with \(L_{j}(a,b)\) altered to another admitted relation for one \((a,b)\notin H\), that transport survives on \(H\) and differs at \((a,b)\), and survival on \(H\) cannot select between the two.

heading: 3. Selected transports are underdetermined on unseen changes their population leaves open
text: Where \(\mathcal T\) contains no such transport, \(H\) is silent on the value at \((a,b)\) and the population fixes it. ∎

heading: 3. Selected transports are underdetermined on unseen changes their population leaves open
label: Consequence
text: **Consequence.** A correspondence produced by selection is faithful where it was tested and, wherever its population admits an alternative, unconstrained where it was not.

heading: 3. Selected transports are underdetermined on unseen changes their population leaves open
label: Consequence
text: This is why the object layer is fallible: it was shaped against the changes its history contained.

heading: 3. Selected transports are underdetermined on unseen changes their population leaves open
label: Consequence
text: It is also why surprise is possible.

heading: 3. Selected transports are underdetermined on unseen changes their population leaves open
label: Consequence
text: What the qualification gives up is the claim of a differing survivor at every unseen pair, and with it the blanket claim that every untested value is unconstrained; a population restriction, a physical relation, or another stated constraint may already fix a value that the history never tested.

heading: 4. Surprise requires an incomplete history
text: ## 4. Surprise requires an incomplete history

heading: 4. Surprise requires an incomplete history
label: Claim
text: **Claim.** A system can be surprised only if it holds a transport selected on a history \(H\) strictly smaller than its contract \(C\).

heading: 4. Surprise requires an incomplete history
text: *Why this and not its denial.*

heading: 4. Surprise requires an incomplete history
text: Surprise is defined (Part IV) as a violation of a selected transport at an occurring \((a,b)\in C\) with \((a,b)\notin H\).

heading: 4. Surprise requires an incomplete history
text: If there is no transport there is no prediction and hence no violation.

heading: 4. Surprise requires an incomplete history
text: If \(H=C\), every such \((a,b)\) is in \(H\), so no violation at a pair of \(C\) outside \(H\) exists. ∎

heading: 4. Surprise requires an incomplete history
label: Consequence
text: **Consequence.** Surprise is not a feeling added to the semantics; it is the signature of a selected transport meeting a change outside its history.

heading: 4. Surprise requires an incomplete history
label: Consequence
text: The two responses, extend \(H\) and re-tune, or construct a new transport, are the difference between learning and creating, and the semantics distinguishes them by their traces, not by their outcomes.

heading: 5. Question-finding is representable
text: ## 5. Question-finding is representable

heading: 5. Question-finding is representable
label: Claim
text: **Claim.** A contract \(C\), taken with its edits and its query, can be given the structure of an organization in the sense of (O), and can be the content \(c\) in (G).

heading: 5. Question-finding is representable
label: Claim
text: Hence an episode whose originative contribution is a new contract meets (G) and, where the other conjuncts are met, (EX).

heading: 5. Question-finding is representable
text: *Why this and not its denial.*

heading: 5. Question-finding is representable
text: A contract is a subset of \(A\times B\) together with \(\mathcal Q\).

heading: 5. Question-finding is representable
text: Give it ports (the edits and their boundaries), components (the closure conditions, each with the relation it imposes on its ports, as (O) requires), and admitted edits (add or remove a change; alter \(\mathcal Q\)).

heading: 5. Question-finding is representable
text: It is then a \(D\) in the sense of (O).

heading: 5. Question-finding is representable
text: Deploy, Build, and New apply. ∎

heading: 5. Question-finding is representable
label: Consequence
text: **Consequence.** Finding a new question, by an owned construction (G), is a creative act, as answering one is.

heading: 5. Question-finding is representable
label: Consequence
text: A semantics that takes questions as inputs cannot represent this; the present one does, by giving contracts provenance.

heading: 5. Question-finding is representable
label: Consequence
text: That a question was found says nothing about how anyone appraises it (Part XI).

heading: 6. There are two imports
text: ## 6. There are two imports

heading: 6. There are two imports
label: Claim
text: **Claim.** Every predicate in Parts II–XIII is defined in terms of \(\Theta\) (including \(\operatorname{Org}_\ell\)) and, where invoked, \(\mathcal N\), together with the structural vocabulary of (O) and (Q), declared indices and declared inputs.

heading: 6. There are two imports
text: *Why this and not its denial.*

heading: 6. There are two imports
text: By the dependence order of Part XIV, which lists the declared indices and the declared inputs with the definitions that use them, following each definition back until it reaches the imports, the indices, the declared inputs, or (O) and (Q), which depend on nothing. ∎

heading: 6. There are two imports
label: Consequence
text: **Consequence.** There is no residual, undefined predicate meaning "explains," "represents," or "is a cause"; (EX) is defined (Part XI).

heading: 6. There are two imports
label: Consequence
text: The two imports are a theory of matter and, when a question requires it, a theory of appraisal.

heading: 6. There are two imports
label: Consequence
text: Neither is a predicate about explanation.

heading: 7. The frozen assessment and the moving question are consistent
text: ## 7. The frozen assessment and the moving question are consistent

heading: 7. The frozen assessment and the moving question are consistent
label: Claim
text: **Claim.** An assessment event with contract \(C\) and an episode in which \(C\) is replaced by \(C'\) with a construction trace are both representable without contradiction.

heading: 7. The frozen assessment and the moving question are consistent
text: *Why this and not its denial.*

heading: 7. The frozen assessment and the moving question are consistent
text: The assessment is indexed to \(C\), and whether \(\mathcal E\) meets (E) on \(C\) is a claim at that index (Part VIII, historical index).

heading: 7. The frozen assessment and the moving question are consistent
text: The episode is a history in which a contract-content \(C'\) is built (Argument 5) and takes over operative use.

heading: 7. The frozen assessment and the moving question are consistent
text: The claim "\(\mathcal E\) is an account on \(C\)" and the claim "\(\mathcal E\) is not an account on \(C'\)" are claims at different indices, and \(\mathcal E\) can meet (E) on \(C\) and fail it on \(C'\). ∎

heading: 7. The frozen assessment and the moving question are consistent
label: Consequence
text: **Consequence.** The point of contact between an explanation and the world moves across episodes because contracts are constructed; it does not move within an assessment because assessments are indexed.

heading: 7. The frozen assessment and the moving question are consistent
label: Consequence
text: Goalpost-moving is the act of passing off a claim at one index as a claim at another; it is not an operation the semantics admits, since every claim is relative to its declared index (Part XIV).

heading: 8. Equivariance under structure-preserving recoding
text: ## 8. Equivariance under structure-preserving recoding

heading: 8. Equivariance under structure-preserving recoding
label: Claim
text: **Claim.** Transporting all carriers, relations, transports, histories, contracts and declared inputs along structure-preserving bijections preserves (E), (G), (P), (EX).

heading: 8. Equivariance under structure-preserving recoding
label: Claim
text: *Why this and not its denial.*

heading: 8. Equivariance under structure-preserving recoding
label: Claim
text: Each is a conjunction of equalities and existence claims over the transported data, the declared aims and occasions of (P) and (EX) among them; bijections preserve them. ∎ The result does not apply to coarsenings, changed boundaries, or lost event identities.

heading: 9. Output descriptions do not determine accounts
label: Claim
text: **Claim.** If \(M_0,M_1\) have the same input–output projection and differ on an account claim, no function of the projection agrees with the claim on both.

heading: 9. Output descriptions do not determine accounts

text: *Why this and not its denial.*

heading: 9. Output descriptions do not determine accounts

heading: 9. Output descriptions do not determine accounts

text: ## 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form
text: Stipulate an object layer \(P\): a line of cells; two things, each with a position and a velocity; continuity components; admitted edits: displace a thing, set its velocity, occlude a cell, swap the two identities.

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form
text: The sensory field is the occupancy of cells, which cells are filled, without which thing fills them.

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form
text: A simulation layer \(S_0\) with a contract \(C_0\) containing the occlusion edit, and a transport \(t_0\) selected on a history \(H_0\subsetneq C_0\) containing displacements and velocity changes but no occlusions.

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form
text: \(S_0\) predicts occupancy from recent occupancy.

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form
text: It is faithful on \(H_0\).

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form
text: \(S_0\), predicting from occupancy, predicts nothing there and is violated when the thing re-emerges at a cell consistent with its velocity.

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form
text: **Construction:** a new organization \(S_1\) is built with a component per thing carrying position and velocity through occlusion, a persistence component, and a transport \(t_1\) from \(P\) whose \(\lambda\) sends each persistence component to a thing's continuity subnetwork.

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form
text: Under (F1), \(t_1\) is faithful on the extended contract.

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form
text: By Argument 1, the persistence components have the signature of things on that contract: they respond to displacement and velocity edits as things do, and are invariant under occlusion as things are.

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form
text: No one declared them to be "objects."

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form
text: On this contract the word adds nothing to the signatures they already have (Argument 1).

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form
text: If \(S_1\) was built by an owned subhistory containing a nontrivial binding construction, the binding of a persistence component to a continuity subnetwork, and \(S_1\) is not in the prior repertoire, then (G) is met.

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form
text: If it repairs the aim "possess a deployable account of re-emergence after occlusion" while protecting "predict the displacements that occur," then (P) is met; and since \(S_1\) is an account on its contract and deployable, (EX) is met.

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form
text: The swap edit is invisible in the sensory field and leaves every prediction unchanged.

heading: 10. A two-layer episode, in exact form
text: On any contract containing it that admits each edit for both things alike, composing \(t_1\) with the exchange of the two things gives a second transport, which sends each persistence component to the other thing's continuity subnetwork.
